extraction.name: Natural Questions (NQ)
extraction.description: Natural Questions is a question answering dataset where questions consist of real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine. An annotator is presented with a question along with a Wikipedia page from the top 5 search results, and annotates a long answer (typically a paragraph) and a short answer (one or more entities) if present on the page, or marks null if no long/short answer is present. The public release consists of 307,373 training examples with single annotations; 7,830 examples with 5-way annotations for development data; and a further 7,842 examples with 5-way annotated sequestered as test data.
extraction.creator: Google Research
extraction.publisher: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics
extraction.citeAs: Kwiatkowski, T., Palomaki, J., Redfield, O., Collins, M., Parikh, A., Alberti, C., Epstein, D., Polosukhin, I., Devlin, J., Lee, K., Toutanova, K., Jones, L., Kelcey, M., Chang, M.-W., Dai, A. M., Uszkoreit, J., Le, Q., & Petrov, S. (2019). Natural Questions: A Benchmark for Question Answering Research. Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 7, 453–466. https://doi.org/10.1162/tacl_a_00276
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Questions consist of real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine. Queries of 8 words or more that have been issued by multiple users in a short period of time are filtered using heuristics to retain fact-seeking questions. The filtered questions are run through the Google search engine and kept only if there is a Wikipedia page in the top 5 search results. The resulting (question, Wikipedia page) pairs are then presented to human annotators who identify long and short answers.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web API, Manual Human Curator, User-generated content data
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: 51% of examples have no answer labeled (long answer is NULL), and 64% have no short answer labeled. Annotators mark NULL when no viable answer candidates exist on the Wikipedia page or when the information required to answer the question is spread across many paragraphs.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine, paired with Wikipedia pages from the top 5 search results for each query.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Simple heuristics are used to filter questions from the query stream: queries must be 8 words or more, issued by multiple users in a short period of time, and must match one of five syntactic/semantic patterns (e.g., starting with 'who', 'when', 'where' followed by specific verb forms, or containing multiple entities with adjectives/adverbs). Questions are further filtered to retain only those where a Wikipedia page appears in the top 5 Google search results.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Questions are filtered from the Google query stream using heuristics to discard non-questions. Part of speech tags and entities are identified using Google's Cloud NLP API. Hearst patterns are used to pre-define categorical noun phrases. Only queries of 8 words or more that match specific syntactic patterns and have a Wikipedia page in the top 5 search results are retained. The dataset is split randomly into train/development/test sets with every question unique under exact string match.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotation is performed using a custom annotation interface by a pool of around 50 annotators, with an average annotation time of 80 seconds. The annotation task is divided into three conceptual stages completed by a single annotator: (1) Question Identification—determining if the question is good (fact-seeking, answerable) or bad (ambiguous, incomprehensible, opinion-seeking, etc.); (2) Long Answer Identification—for good questions, selecting the earliest HTML bounding box (paragraph, table, list item, or whole list) containing enough information to infer the answer, or marking 'no answer'; (3) Short Answer Identification—for examples with long answers, selecting the entity or set of entities within the long answer that answer the question, or flagging yes/no/no short answer possible. Post hoc evaluation of annotation quality was performed by four experts who independently annotated examples for correctness (Correct, Correct but debatable, Wrong) and then reached consensus judgments.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Annotation quality was evaluated via post hoc expert review of 139 sampled non-null examples, yielding 90% precision for long answers and 84% for short answers. 25-way annotations on 302 examples were collected to study variability. The proportion of non-null annotations (mu) was found to be highly correlated with annotation precision. For examples where more than 80% of 25 annotators gave a non-null answer, expert judgments were overwhelmingly correct. Disagreement between annotators was largely accounted for by the 'Correct but debatable' category. The most popular long answer accounts for 83% of long answer annotations; the most popular short answer accounts for 64% of short answer annotations.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Training set: 1 annotation per item; Development set: 5 annotations per item; Test set: 5 annotations per item; Quality evaluation subset: 25 annotations per item (302 examples)
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Google's Cloud NLP API (for part of speech tags and entity identification); Hearst patterns (for identifying categorical noun phrases)
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Questions are real but anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is designed to drive research in natural language understanding and open-domain question answering, with genuine utility to users seeking information. A solution to Natural Questions would have real-world utility as an information-seeking question answering system.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset focuses on Wikipedia as the evidence source, which may introduce biases inherent to Wikipedia's content and coverage. The dataset focuses on longer queries (8+ words) and excludes 'how to' questions. Future data collection efforts may introduce shorter queries, 'how to' questions, or domains other than Wikipedia.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset focuses only on Wikipedia as the evidence source, which may not generalize to other domains. Only queries of 8 words or more are included, excluding shorter queries. 'How to' questions are excluded. Boolean answers are not addressed in the baseline experiments and are left to future work. The dataset may have biases due to the choice of Wikipedia as the evidence source. List-formatted long answers are underrepresented (6% of non-null examples), leading to lower model performance on this type.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training (307,373 examples with single annotations), Validation/Development (7,830 examples with 5-way annotations), and Testing (7,842 examples with 5-way annotations) for question answering systems. The dataset is intended as a benchmark for evaluating QA and natural language understanding systems, particularly for end-to-end open-domain question answering.
